## Work in progress

### Why Don't Deposits Move? Depositor Inertia and Deposit Competition in Brazilian Retail Banking

*Draft, October 2026* · [Code](https://github.com/PFeijodeMoraes23/Deposit_Competition_Code)

Brazilian depositors leave most of their balances in accounts that pay well below
the policy rate, even though better-paying deposits are one transfer away and the
Pix instant-payment system made that transfer free. I ask which friction keeps them
in place: inattention, unawareness of alternatives, the cost of moving, or an
informed preference to stay.

I extend the dynamic deposit model of Egan, Hortaçsu, Kaplan, Sunderam, and Yao
(2025) to a market where brick-and-mortar banks compete locally and digital banks
nationally, with random-coefficients (BLP) demand. Estimation proceeds in two steps
on a municipality-level panel of bank balances built from Banco Central do Brasil
supervisory data (2016–2024): depositor sleepiness from the persistence of deposits,
with a control function for endogenous spreads, and demand from a BLP contraction.

**Preliminary findings**

- Over a full year, {{< var paper.sleep_yoy >}} percent of balances are never
  re-optimized ({{< var paper.sleep_qoq >}} percent in a given quarter), and inertia
  is deeper in poorer markets.
- Active depositors' mean own-price elasticity is {{< var paper.elast_active >}}, but
  because most balances are asleep, the deposit base responds to a spread change on
  impact with an elasticity of only {{< var paper.elast_impact >}}. This gap is the
  market power that inertia gives incumbent banks.
- The launch of Pix is associated with a reduction in the sleepy share of
  {{< var paper.pix_shift >}} percentage points, not distinguishable from zero
  (95 percent interval [{{< var paper.pix_ci_lo >}}, {{< var paper.pix_ci_hi >}}]).
  The interval is too wide to rule out a large rise in the share of depositors
  who shop.
- A market's 2019 mobile access predicts its Pix use, which gives a first step
  toward separating attention from the cost of moving money.

## Research assistance

**Dirk Bergemann, Yale University** (2023–2024). Information sharing between
consumers and producers through a data intermediary, comparing for-profit and
consumer-fiduciary intermediaries; an information-design model of screening with
two quality levels.

**Humberto Moreira and Marcelo Sant'Anna, FGV EPGE** (2021–2022). Demand for
automobile insurance in Brazil: a duopoly model with consumers heterogeneous in
risk and insurer preference, using SUSEP regulatory data (2010–2020), and a report
on market power, screening, and mergers.
